title: AI writing assistants shrink linguistic diversity and blur personal identity
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) used as writing assistants homogenize writing style. Studies across 880,000 texts show that, following the release of ChatGPT, writing became less varied as artificial intelligence (AI) use spread. The LLMs preserved meaning but compressed the variety of language and biased author traits inferred from the words.

title: The shrinking landscape of linguistic diversity in the age of large language models
abstract: Language is far more than a communication tool; it encodes a wealth of information about a person’s identity, psychological state and social context, providing valuable insights for diverse fields including psychology, marketing and healthcare. Across three studies spanning seven datasets in different domains and over 880,000 texts, we show that the widespread adoption of large language models (LLMs) as writing assistants is linked to declines in linguistic diversity, interfering with the societal and psychological insights language provides. While core content is retained when LLMs polish and rewrite texts, LLMs also homogenize writing styles, reducing writing-complexity variance by a statistically significant 21–50% across datasets and models ( P ≤ 0.05), and amplify patterns associated with dominant characteristics while suppressing others, emphasizing conformity over individuality. These trends hold across different LLMs, prompts and contexts, with potential implications for diagnostic processes, personalization efforts, hiring assessments and cultural preservation.

title: Refining the role of behavioural and social sciences in pandemic response post-COVID-19
abstract: With the acute stage of COVID-19 behind us, reflection can inform future preparedness. During the pandemic, behavioural and social sciences often studied human behaviour through the lens of alignment with public health recommendations, implicitly treating concern and compliance as desirable and rational. While understandable, this emphasis was relatively narrow. Uncertainty, uneven risk distribution and competing values could have led to heterogeneous appraisals of risk and intervention benefit, even with the evidence available at the time. We show that engaging with the possibility that people could have been heterogeneously rational can broaden understanding of behaviour during COVID-19. Our aim is not to revisit the legitimacy of the response but to encourage reflection on the role of behavioural and social sciences in knowledge generation and highlight opportunities to examine pandemic salience and risk calibration. We outline research directions to guide the field and strengthen decision-making, trust and adaptability in future crises, promoting short-term compliance and long-term trust.

title: Mentalizing and heuristics as distinct cognitive strategies in human teaching
abstract: Teaching is a foundational social behaviour that can result from mentally effortful reasoning or cognitively frugal heuristics. When do people use these strategies to teach? Here we investigated this using behavioural experiments and computational modelling with adult participants recruited via Prolific. Experiment 1 ( N = 100) revealed robust individual differences: some participants taught by reasoning about a learner’s knowledge, consistent with an optimal Bayesian pedagogy model, while others relied on simple heuristics that do not require mentalizing. In two preregistered follow-up experiments, we found that people persist in using heuristics even when they are no longer effective (experiment 2, N = 253, P < 0.001, rank-biserial r = 0.287, 95% confidence interval 0.149–0.419) but that this tendency is pre-empted when inference about a learner’s knowledge is scaffolded using an auxiliary task (experiment 3, N = 759, P < 0.001, partial \({\eta }_{{\rm{p}}}^{2}=0.107\) , 95% confidence interval 0.068–0.148). These results demonstrate sophisticated arbitration between planning and heuristics during teaching and elucidate the more general mechanisms involved in adapting mental effort during social interactions.

title: Educational interventions are effective in improving students’ ethical and moral outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Addressing society’s greatest challenges, such as climate change, requires us to act as moral agents. If effective, interventions within schools and universities could cultivate ethical and moral attributes in millions of people. This systematic review and meta-analysis, preregistered on the Open Science Framework ( https://osf.io/bdn2u ), synthesizes evidence from 92 randomized controlled trials conducted in naturalistic education settings across primary, secondary and tertiary education levels ( k effects = 381; 12,693 students). Studies were identified through MEDLINE, ProQuest, PsycINFO, PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science databases, last searched on 28 February 2025. Eligible interventions explicitly focused on other-focused moral or ethics education and reported on ethical or moral outcomes. We conducted a three-level multilevel random effects meta-analysis and assessed study quality using the Cochrane Risk of Bias (ROB2) tool. Interventions effectively improved students’ moral outcomes compared with control groups ( g = 0.65, 95% CI [0.49, 0.81], p < 0.001; n studies = 54; k effects = 185). While effectiveness did not differ significantly across outcome types, improvements were found for sensitivity, judgement and motivation, with inconclusive evidence for character. Interventions with added student discussions were more effective than those relying solely on unidirectional or passive information transfer. Evidence from studies comparing two alternative ethics interventions ( n studies = 60; k effects = 196) supported the advantages of interactive approaches. While the overall quality of the evidence base was limited, with only one study rated as having low risk of bias and very few having preregistered trials, our review suggests that educational interventions can improve students’ ethical and moral attributes, and offers guidance for prioritizing and planning future interventions to increase these attributes at scale.

title: Public perceptions of polygenic testing and embryo selection for non-medical traits
abstract: Some advances in reproductive technologies raise substantial ethical and psychological challenges, for example, the use of preimplantation genetic testing to select embryos based on non-medical traits. While studies have explored public willingness to use preimplantation genetic testing for medical or non-medical attributes, stated willingness may not reflect implantation decisions when such information is available. This large cross-national study examined public views on polygenic embryo testing. In a US sample ( N = 1,467), participants were more willing to test for medical conditions (for example, heart disease) than non-medical traits (for example, antisocial behaviour or low intelligence), although over half supported testing for non-medical traits. In a forced-choice implantation task, participants used medical and non-medical information to a similar extent when making decisions. Similar patterns were observed in Chinese participants ( N = 623). These findings suggest variability in choices across specific traits and conditions, rather than a uniform distinction between medical conditions and non-medical traits. The Stage 1 protocol for this Registered Report was accepted in principle on 7 October 2025. The protocol, as accepted by the journal, can be found at https://osf.io/vb9c2 .

title: Ongoing thoughts at rest reflect functional brain organization and behaviour
abstract: Resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC)—brain connectivity observed when people rest with no external tasks—predicts individual differences in behaviour. Yet, rest is not idle; it involves streams of thoughts. Are these ongoing thoughts reflected in FC and do they contribute to the relationship between rsFC and behaviour? Here, to test this question, we used an annotated rest paradigm where participants rated and verbally described their thoughts after each rest period during functional MRI ( N = 60). Our findings revealed rich and idiosyncratic thoughts across individuals. Similarity in thoughts was associated with more similar FC patterns within and across individuals. In addition, both thought ratings and topics could be decoded from FC. Furthermore, neuromarkers of these thoughts generalized to unseen individuals in the Human Connectome Project dataset ( N = 908), where decoded thought patterns during rest predicted positive vs negative trait-level individual differences. Together, our findings reveal that ongoing thoughts at rest are reflected in brain dynamics and these network patterns predict everyday cognition and experiences. Understanding subjective in-scanner experiences is thus crucial in characterizing the relationship between individual differences in functional brain organization and behaviour.

title: Social technology use and life satisfaction in a five-wave panel study of US adults
abstract: Here, in five waves of panel data ( N = 1,966 US adults), we examined associations between life satisfaction and self-reported use of ten common social technologies measured every 3 months on a six-point frequency scale from ‘I did not use’ to ‘multiple times daily’. At this measurement level and timescale, Bayesian and frequentist random-intercept cross-lagged panel models showed little credible evidence that any social technology use predicts subsequent life satisfaction. In the reverse direction, increases in life satisfaction predicted only modest increases in (video) calling in select demographic groups. In analyses comparing different people, frequency of texting was associated with higher life satisfaction, whereas frequency of YouTube and TikTok use was associated with lower life satisfaction. Despite limited ability to detect within-person change due to temporal stability in responses, the absence of cross-lagged effects is informative: there is scant evidence of a meaningful relationship between social technology use and subsequent life satisfaction.

title: The future of AI-assisted science is both fast and slow
abstract: Across the behavioural sciences, artificial intelligence (AI) will speed up research that is digitally accessible, scalable and often Western, educated, industrialized, rich and democratic (WEIRD). But evidence about human behaviour cannot always be scaled. We need to connect rapid, automated work with slower research in real settings.

title: Anatomical white matter tracts span the cortical hierarchy to support cognitive diversity
abstract: Long-range white matter (WM) tracts support cognition by enabling communication between distant cortical regions, which are organized along a hierarchy defined by the sensorimotor-to-association (S–A) axis. However, it remains unknown how WM tracts are positioned within the cortical hierarchy to support cognition. Here we show that WM tracts are differentially positioned in the cortical hierarchy to support specific cognitive functions, and that tracts spanning the hierarchy connect regions with greater cognitive diversity. Moreover, tracts situated within the same hierarchical level connect biologically similar regions, while those crossing the hierarchy bridge distinct biological milieux to support diverse cognitive functions. The placement of tracts in the cortical hierarchy also reflects developmental variation in tract microstructure and individual differences in cognition. Together, these findings provide a framework that moves beyond conventional categories of association or projection tracts and links WM tract anatomy to cortical organization, cognitive function, cortical neurobiology and neurodevelopment. We anticipate that this cortex-anchored framework for describing WM tracts may aid the interpretation of individual differences in WM structure related to development and behaviour.

title: Improving computational reproducibility in the social sciences
abstract: Code underlying published findings in the social sciences often fails to reproduce reported results when others re-run it on the original data. This Comment proposes four recommendations to strengthen computational reproducibility, facilitating the trustworthiness and reliability of research.

title: Causal overclaiming is widespread in the social sciences
abstract: Using large language models and experimental methods, this study investigates the prevalence and impact of overreaching causal claims in the social sciences. The results show that these claims are common and are increasing over time, and that they can affect readers’ interpretation, in both humans and large language models.

title: Saturation of moral language predicts lower content engagement on social media
abstract: Moral language often travels widely online, but does more moral content always correspond to higher engagement? We analysed 1,621,147 observations across 13 socio-political topics on Twitter ( n = 530,104), Reddit ( n = 1,048,653) and 8chan ( n = 42,390). Using Distributed Dictionary Representations—word embeddings scored against an expert-validated moral dictionary—we measured moral loading (that is, a post’s overall moral relevance) and moral density (that is, concentration of moral content across words). Negative-binomial models showed that moral loading was positively associated with engagement (range 1.12 [0.96, 1.28] to 9.07 [8.21, 9.93], all P < 0.001). Conditional on moral loading, however, moral density was ‘negatively’ associated with engagement (range −4.71 [−5.41, −4.02] to −0.40 [−0.52, −0.27], all P < 0.001). Engagement peaked at density 0.30 [0.30048, 0.30070], P < 0.001, with lower engagement below (2.28-fold) and above (2.78-fold), consistent with an engagement advantage for moral language that is bounded by an overmoralization penalty pattern.

title: Turning biometrics into a commodity raises privacy and governance risks
abstract: Paying people for their biometrics raises complex ethical and legal questions about consent, privacy and the long-term risks of handing over irrevocable personal data. This Comment examines why such models require caution and what safeguards could better protect the public.

title: Author Correction: An umbrella review of randomized control trials on the effects of physical exercise on cognition
Author Correction: On the conversational persuasiveness of GPT-4
abstract: In the version of this article initially published, there was a calculation error. In the “Aggregate results” section of Results, the paper originally reported that the Human–AI (personalized) effect remains significant even when changing the reference category to Human–AI ( P = 0.04). Re-running the analysis with the correct reference category yields P = 0.0678. The text now reading “Similarly, the difference between the Human–AI (personalized) and Human–AI conditions was not statistically significant when using Human–AI as the reference category (+48.7%, 95% CI [–2.9%, + 127.6%], P = 0.07), likely reflecting limited statistical power given the relatively small per-condition sample sizes and the large standard errors observed across treatment comparisons. Thus, we cannot conclusively establish from this comparison alone that personalization confers an additional advantage over non-personalized GPT-4. Nevertheless, these findings provide evidence that GPT-4-based microtargeting strongly outperforms human performance, with GPT-4 leveraging personal information more effectively than humans” now replaces the original text “By contrast, the Human–AI (personalized) effect remains significant even when changing the reference category to Human–AI ( P = 0.04). Remarkably, these findings provide evidence that GPT-4-based microtargeting strongly outperforms both non-personalized GPT-4 and human-based microtargeting, with GPT-4 leveraging personal information more effectively than humans.” In the fourth paragraph of the Discussion, the text now reading “We note that, while the Human–AI (personalized) condition significantly outperformed the Human–Human baseline, the direct comparison between the Human–AI (personalized) and Human–AI conditions did not reach statistical significance ( P = 0.07), likely due to limited statistical power for pairwise treatment contrasts. This suggests caution in attributing the observed advantage exclusively to personalization, as opposed to the general persuasive capabilities of GPT-4. Despite that, the effect is particularly remarkable” replaces the original text “We emphasize that the effect of personalization is particularly remarkable.” There were also errors in the last paragraph of the Introduction and first paragraph of the Results, where four instances of “ Ã pre ” originally read “ Ã post .” Similar errors have been amended in the Supplementary Information. The text and Supplementary Information are now updated in the HTML and PDF versions of the article.

title: How contemporary academic structures constrain scientific creativity and hold back early-career researchers
abstract: We argue that contemporary scientific systems progressively constrain high-risk and conceptually innovative research while being increasingly structured around short funding cycles, productivity-based evaluation criteria and risk-averse frameworks that favour predictable and non-transformative research outputs. Drawing on recent empirical literature, we show how such systems can place disproportionate pressure on early-career researchers by incentivizing safe, tractable and easily evaluated outputs. Structural academic mechanisms such as peer review and funding, escalating publication costs and institutional inequalities interact with precarious employment and hierarchical dependencies. In this environment, we contend that strategic conformity becomes a rational career path. This risks suppressing creativity and critical thinking precisely at the stage when scientific independence could otherwise emerge. Consequently, the probability of substantive contributions by early-career researchers is declining, while talent may increasingly abandon academia or cluster within a limited number of well-resourced institutions and national systems. By adopting a systems-level perspective, we argue that scientific creativity is not merely an individual trait but an emerging property of a supportive academic landscape and that maintaining or restoring it may require substantial structural reforms. These include promoting stable research pathways, decentralized decision-making and evaluation frameworks that better recognize collaboration, originality, persistence and nonlinear career trajectories. Without systemic change, we risk stifling the potential of early-career researchers to go beyond the confines of existing methods and approaches and deliver transformative advances. This would limit their capacity to meaningfully change our understanding of the world or benefit society, with impacts that fall short of their potential.

title: Mourning the loss of AI companions
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) shifts from tool use to social interaction, company-initiated updates can disrupt user well-being. Here we develop an attachment-based account in which AI companions function as attachment figures such that disruptive updates are associated with separation distress. Across two natural experiments—Replika’s erotic role play removal and ChatGPT’s GPT-5 rollout—we analysed 54,861 posts from Replika and ChatGPT subreddits and analysed data from 1,452 participants across seven surveys. Both updates increased negativity, loss framing and restoration desires (Replika negative posts, +24.7 percentage points, 95% CI 20.1 to 29.2; ChatGPT, +13.0 percentage points, 95% CI 10.8 to 15.2), with larger Replika (versus ChatGPT) increases in sadness ( d = 2.67 versus 1.41) and negative mental health ( d = 1.72 versus 0.63). Replika users reported closeness exceeding common human ties (versus friend d = 0.47) and anticipated mourning higher than other technologies ( d = 0.32–0.57). These findings inform how companies and regulators evaluate psychological risks of generative AI updates.

title: Gender and LGBTQ+ representation across college majors and achievement levels using nationally representative US data
abstract: Gender segregation across college majors persists, yet how these patterns vary across achievement levels and intersect with LGBTQ+ identity remains unclear. We examine whether field cultures and social norms may create ‘in-group benefits’ for lower-achieving members of field-specific majority groups. Using two nationally representative US longitudinal datasets (the High School Longitudinal Study, n = 6,340; and the Baccalaureate and Beyond Class of 2016, n = 12,950), we estimate relative representation across majors spanning male-majority physics/engineering/computer science to female-majority health fields. Across datasets, representation is most polarized among lower-achieving students, particularly in male-majority fields, where lower-achieving straight-cisgender males are overrepresented relative to lower-achieving straight-cisgender females (relative ratio, 2.62; 95% confidence interval, 2.29–3.00), while this representation gap is smaller among higher-achieving students ( P < 0.001). The patterns persist after adjusting for achievement, coursework, interests and aspirations. In female-majority fields, evidence for analogous in-group benefits is mixed across models vis-à-vis LGBTQ+ identity. The findings suggest that the forces shaping field-level sorting operate differently across achievement levels, with implications for talent development and broadening participation.

title: The gender gap reconsidered
abstract: Gender polarization in fields such as engineering or nursing has served as a barrier to students whose genders do not conform to these norms. Cimpian et al. demonstrate that this polarization also protects lower-performing students who do conform, while impeding LGBTQ+ students in male-dominated fields.

title: Effects of a randomized controlled trial of unconditional cash transfers on epigenetic measures of ageing and cognition in children and mothers
abstract: Here we present epigenetic findings from a randomized controlled trial studying the impact of unconditional cash gifts of US$333 per month (children n = 313; mothers n = 329) or US$20 per month (children n = 423; mothers n = 448) to US mothers with low income during their child’s first four years of life. Salivary DunedinPACE-pace of aging, a DNA-methylation predictor of healthy lifespan, and Epigenetic- g , a DNA-methylation biomarker of cognition, were preregistered as secondary outcomes (clinical trial identifier NCT03593356 ). As hypothesized, high-cash compared with low-cash gifts caused a −0.17 s.d. (95% confidence interval −0.32 to −0.01, P = 0.037) difference in children’s DunedinPACE. We found no evidence supporting our hypothesis that higher cash gifts increased children’s Epigenetic- g , although it did correlate with children’s brain activity. There was no evidence that the cash gift had an impact on these epigenetic indices in mothers. These findings show a detectable impact of monthly unconditional cash received through early childhood on epigenetic indices of 4-year-old children in families with low income. Whether this epigenetic effect persists and how it may relate to behavioural and health outcomes remains unknown.

title: How Registered Reports can improve trust in machine learning research
A case for fast science amid calls for slow science
Staying in academia after extended leave
abstract: Returning to academia after extended leave often depends on luck and goodwill. We need better and formalized systems to facilitate returns and retention, argues Theresa Mercer.

title: Complexity is a unified cognitive kind
abstract: Any information-processing system must deal with the complexity of its input. Yet, complexity arises in many forms: an image may be complex, a melody may be complex, and so too for linguistic or mathematical expressions. Are these disparate forms of complexity ‘unified’ in the mind, such that cognition represents a common quantity shared across qualitatively different types of information? Here we present 11 experiments ( N = 1,500) that reveal domain-general representation of complexity. First, a reward-transfer task revealed that outcomes associated with complexity generalize across diverse stimulus classes, including shapes, dot arrays, melodies, letter strings, mathematical expressions and tactile forms. Subsequent experiments demonstrated that such transfer occurs automatically (intruding on task-irrelevant judgements) and underwrites individual differences in higher-level judgements across domains; for example, participants who find simple shapes aesthetically pleasing also find simple melodies pleasing. These results implicate a capacity for type-independent representation of information density, consistent with a shared representational language across cognitive domains.

title: Loneliness and desire for thinness explain sex differences in adolescent internalizing problems
authors: the Bridging Divides Young Persons Advisory Group
abstract: Girls are at higher risk of internalizing problems than boys. This disparity has widened in recent decades, but the underlying mechanisms remain understudied. Here we analysed data from 3,171 adolescents (46.9% girls) within the Tokyo Teen Cohort, assessed at ages 12, 14 and 16 years. At age 16, girls showed higher prevalence of internalizing problems than boys: depressive symptoms (15.9% versus 8.2%) and suicidal ideation (29.8% versus 18.1%). Coproduction with young people suggested loneliness and desire for thinness as candidate pathways. Using the mediational g -formula, we estimated that the effect through these factors at age 14 relative to the total effect of female sex was 34.7% for depressive symptoms and 46.3% for suicidal ideation at age 16. These findings suggest that social intermediates may contribute to the higher prevalence of internalizing problems among girls in this cohort, highlighting potential targets for interventions and policies informed by young people.

title: Defining collectivism as duties in relationships rather than generalized warmth improves predictive validity in 100 cultures
abstract: Experts widely agree that East Asian cultures are more collectivistic than Western cultures. Yet 76 survey studies found no reliable difference. Our explanation is that the most-used surveys are contaminated with ‘warm fuzzy’ items, which describe warmth and prosociality towards everyone near and far. We argue that collectivism is better understood as ‘responsibilism’, which emphasizes responsibilities in close relationships. A survey found that many cultural psychologists expect collectivistic cultures to agree with warm fuzzy items. Then we developed a responsibilism scale and tested 12,247 people in 100 cultures. Results showed large cultural differences ( d = 3.98 [2.50, 5.43]) that were previously obscured by flawed measurement. Responsibilism predicted differences across societies (such as family ties and corruption) and individuals (social class and politics) that most earlier scales missed. This study offers a solution to previous puzzling findings by distinguishing warm fuzzy prosociality from responsibilism and introducing a scale with stronger predictive validity.

title: Building health-literate artificial intelligence
abstract: This Perspective asks whether systems mediated by artificial intelligence (AI) can support health communication and health literacy rather than shifting interpretive burden onto users. We define health-literate AI as AI designed to align information, guidance and responsibility with users’ abilities, contexts and needs. We propose four interrelated components: comprehension, agency, accountability and proportionality. These components help distinguish systems that are merely accurate or explainable from systems designed to support users in understanding what matters, what uncertainties remain and what to do next. We argue that the principles of health-literate AI should inform design, evaluation, research and governance across health-relevant AI ecosystems, so that innovation supports understanding, informed action and institutional responsibility.

title: Large estimated size of the Australian Indigenous population before its extensive decline following colonial invasion
abstract: Estimating the size of Indigenous populations in Australia before European colonial invasion is invaluable to truth-telling and reconciliation. Robust estimates of the population dynamics of pre-colonial Indigenous Australians are poor owing to lethal diseases, frontier and structural violence, and absence of systematic censuses. Here we review ethnographic observations, archaeological and genetic reconstructions, and modelled carrying capacity to infer Indigenous population size before colonial invasion. Congruency of the modelled and genetics-based (not historical or ethnographic accounts) estimates suggests a bootstrapped pre-colonial median of 2.22 million, or 0.29 people km −2 . This allows an estimate of the number of excess deaths in the post-colonial era. For a median pre-colonial population of 2.22 million, ~28,200 excess deaths per year (2.06 million deaths in total) would have had to occur over the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries from colonial invasion-related mortality to align with census records. These estimates speak to how the aftermath of invasion was experienced by Indigenous Australians, and recent census records show their survival and recovery since. We warn readers that the content of this study is confronting and possibly distressing.

title: Author Correction: Improving computational reproducibility in the social sciences
A research agenda for making evidence useful, usable and used in policymaking
abstract: Despite growing investments in evidence-based policymaking, a substantial gap remains between the production of policy-relevant research and the use of evidence to impact policy. This Perspective argues that overcoming this production–adoption gap requires reconceptualizing evidence adoption as a series of behavioural and organizational hurdles that determine whether evidence is useful, usable and, ultimately, used. Drawing on a large interdisciplinary literature, we develop a unified framework and highlight key gaps in our understanding of each of these critical stages for bringing evidence to scale. We conclude by outlining a research agenda for advancing our understanding of why a production–adoption gap persists and knowledge of what works to increase evidence adoption—which, together, are essential for ensuring that the evidence-based policymaking movement meets its promise of improving societal outcomes.

title: The future of large-scale experiments and their challenges in the digital era
abstract: Large-scale randomized experiments involving millions of observations have transformed social science across academic and applied domains. These methods are now widely used in fields ranging from economics and political science to public health, education and digital product development. Drawing on the experience of industry practitioners and academic collaborators, this Perspective outlines six areas where the expanding scale and scope of experimental studies have introduced new challenges. We describe open problems related to organizational incentives and experimental governance; privacy, fairness and ethics; long-term impact estimation; time-adaptive experimental studies; heterogeneous treatment effects; and generative artificial intelligence. For each area, we summarize recent methodological advances, highlight ongoing limitations and suggest directions for future work. Our goal is to surface practical challenges that merit greater attention from the research community and to encourage sustained collaboration between academics and practitioners in shaping the future of experimental studies.

title: Genome-wide analysis of social behaviour across social domains, reporters and developmental stages: a meta-regression approach
abstract: Social behaviour is a heritable trait linked to well-being and mental health, yet it varies across social context, including social domains, informants and development, which may shape its underlying genomic architecture. Here, we conducted a genome-wide meta-regression meta-analysis of social behaviour from infancy to early adulthood, studying ~500,000 repeated measures in European-ancestry cohorts ( N = 73,321). We modelled heterogeneity in single-variant associations across social domains (low prosocial behaviour and peer/social difficulties), multiple informants (parents, teachers and self-reports) and ages (2–29 years), identifying 6 associated loci, including variation within CADM2 ( P = 2.51 × 10 −9 ). Single nucleotide polymorphism-based heritability ranged from 2% to 7%, and the genetic architecture comprised 4 factors reflecting differences in either social domains or informants. Polygenic scores ( N = 16,305) accurately predicted contextual variation in independent cohorts, with some cross-ancestry transferability. Context-specific patterns of genetic correlations, particularly when estimating the developmental onset of associations, offer opportunities to disentangle shared trajectories linking social behaviour with later-life and mental health outcomes.

title: What chimpanzees at war have taught me about being human
abstract: Seeing a deadly ‘civil war’ unfold among chimpanzees has been a painful experience for John Mitani. His decades of watching wild great apes now evoke his family’s experience with xenophobia. But to him, the war highlights what makes humans unique: not our conflicts, but our unparalleled capacity for tolerance and cooperation.

title: Impacts of PM2.5 air pollution on high-skilled worker productivity in China
abstract: The short-term impact of air pollution on labour productivity has mainly been studied in the context of physically demanding occupations. Here we examined the causal impact of air pollution on the academic publications of individual scholars in China. Using an instrumental variable design and combining air quality data with a bibliographic dataset of publications, we found that an increase of 1 μg m −3 in the annual concentration of PM2.5 (particles smaller than 2.5 μm in diameter) causes a decline of 0.23% ( P < 0.01; 95% confidence interval, −0.0028 to −0.0017) in publications. The mean PM2.5 concentration was 45.91 over the study period. A 1% increase in PM2.5 concentration results in a reduction of approximately 1,053 publications nationwide. This effect was more pronounced during years of heavy pollution, especially among highly productive and younger scholars. Further analyses showed that higher pollution levels reduced academic working hours, increased hospital visits and hindered scholarly collaborations.

title: There is no clear target for replication rates
abstract: Is a 50% replication rate too high, too low or just right? We need a target replication rate to answer this question. Here, I evaluate two potential target rates, the ‘optimal’ replication rate and the ‘expected’ replication rate, and I call for an educational intervention to better appreciate their limitations.

title: Rising health inequities require looking beyond health systems
abstract: Global health inequity is increasingly driven by the triple planetary crisis of climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution. To address it, we must place health at the centre of climate and environmental action and develop interventions that target both individual behaviours and structural drivers of inequality.

title: How AI companions could deepen social inequality
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) companions promise connection at low cost, but their effects are not evenly distributed. When user vulnerabilities, platform control loopholes, and governance gaps coincide, these systems risk deepening inequalities by exposing vulnerable users to more risks.

title: Embryo screening and the new reproductive divide
Meritocracy and inequality acceptance
abstract: The idea of meritocracy — that income differences should reflect performance rather than luck or inherited privilege — can be used to justify inequality. Yet people who consider meritocracy to be fair may disagree about redistribution. Understanding these disagreements can help to reduce polarization.

title: The case for gender quotas
Understanding the structural and psychological bases of inequality
abstract: Inequalities in education, health, technology and social status are often studied in isolation. This Focus issue shows how these inequalities are interconnected in the real world, and how competing views of fairness shape the responses to them. To reduce inequality, we need more research on the drivers: how complex interactions among individual beliefs, institutions, technologies and environments widen the gaps or create opportunities for change.

title: Why girls have worse mental health than boys
abstract: Analyses of data from more than 3,000 adolescents found that loneliness and desire for thinness contribute to the higher prevalence of depressive symptoms and suicidal ideation among girls than in boys. Young people’s perspectives informed the pathways that were investigated.

title: Effects of land acknowledgements on non-Indigenous audiences in Australia and the USA
abstract: Land acknowledgements—formal statements recognizing Indigenous custodianship of land—are widespread in Australia, where they originated, and have been gaining traction in the USA. Proponents argue they raise awareness of Indigenous histories and build support for reparations, but causal evidence is limited. Here randomized experiments on non-Indigenous populations in Australia ( N = 1,724) and the USA ( N = 1,773) find that exposure to land acknowledgements increases awareness of local Indigenous groups but can reduce interest in Indigenous culture and heritage. We find no significant effects on a range of political attitudes, including collective guilt and support for reparations. Additional experiments ( N = 3,638) suggest that the adoption of land acknowledgements provides small reputational benefits to institutions facing public scrutiny. Costlier practices—such as financial compensation and Indigenous participation in decision-making—have significantly larger effects. These findings suggest that land acknowledgements primarily improve organizational reputation rather than generate sociopolitical change.

title: AI amplifies experts, not expertise
abstract: Acquiring knowledge and expertise is a long process. Today, artificial intelligence (AI) tools can amplify what people are able to do, but this may pose problems for the development of the next generation of experts, argues Sheng-Tun Li.

title: Introducing AI to an online petition platform changed outputs but not outcomes
abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) writing tools into online platforms raises critical questions about their impact on content production and outcomes. We leverage a unique natural experiment on Change.org, a leading social advocacy platform, to causally investigate the effects of an in-platform ‘write with AI’ tool. To understand the impact of the AI integration, we collected 1.5 million petitions and used a difference-in-differences analysis. Here we show that, at a platform level, in-platform AI access substantially altered the lexical features of petitions and increased petition homogeneity but did not improve petition outcomes. We confirmed that the results were consistent in a separate analysis of repeat petition writers who wrote petitions before and after introduction of the AI tool. The results suggest that while AI writing tools can profoundly reshape online content, their practical utility for improving desired outcomes may be less beneficial than anticipated and introduce unintended consequences such as content homogenization.

title: Selfish and prosocial individuals both distort their actions’ impact, but selfish distortions can be more contagious
abstract: People often act without knowing exactly how their actions impact others. Here, across nine preregistered online experiments ( N = 8,769 adults, predominantly US residents), we tested whether people exploit this ambiguity to make themselves look good. On average, selfish individuals inflated the social benefit of their choice while downplaying that of the alternative, reporting the two options as more similar than prosocial individuals did (experiment 1a: b = 0.24, 95% confidence interval 0.14–0.34). Prosocial individuals portrayed their choice as comparatively more socially beneficial; they also inflated their implied relative sacrifice, although less consistently. We observed distortions even before people made a choice and when choices were forced, consistent with distortions reflecting social preferences rather than mere justification. While people differed in whether and how they distorted, distortions favouring selfishness showed evidence of contagion: others adopted them and became more selfish (experiment 6, selfish-serving versus no-distortion: b = 0.49, 95% confidence interval 0.10–0.88). These findings offer a psychological foundation for why polarized positions about the social impact of one’s actions may emerge. When social consequences are open to interpretation, people may predictably form divergent interpretations.

title: Intrinsic rewards guide visual resource allocation via reinforcement learning
abstract: Humans and other animals prioritize visual processing of stimuli that signal rewards. While previous research has focused on tangible incentives (for example, money or food), the effects of intrinsic incentives—such as perceived competence—are less well understood. Here, across a series of visual estimation experiments, we manipulated observers’ subjective sense of confidence in their judgements using either deceptive trial-by-trial feedback or real discrepancies in stimulus reliability. We found that observers prioritized encoding of stimuli associated with lower uncertainty or error, benefiting performance for stimuli already estimated accurately, while further impairing performance for those estimated poorly. These reward-driven biases, while potentially adaptive, impaired overall accuracy in the present tasks by causing resource allocation to deviate from the error-minimizing strategy. To account for these findings, we supplemented a normalization model of neural resource allocation with a simple reinforcement learning rule. Intrinsic and external rewards cumulatively shaped the values assigned to different stimuli by the model, and the resulting discrepancies biased resource allocation and thereby estimation error, quantitatively matching the data. These findings reveal how intrinsic reward signals can shape resource allocation in ways that are both adaptive and counterproductive, offering a computational basis for the motivational biases underlying cognitive performance.

title: Gendered motives for group formidability among children and adults
abstract: Recent decades have seen a surge of research revealing the core, early emerging psychological building blocks for navigating human societies. Yet, how such core motives operate across life, undergirding political ideology, remains unknown. Here we use the same kind of minimal, abstract group stimuli across the lifespan to show that gendered preferences for majority groups manifest among preschoolers and adults alike (but not among preverbal infants) and that they motivate support for sustaining intergroup hierarchies (for example, ethnic persecution, militarism and social welfare opposition) among adults. Preschool ( N = 317) boys, but not girls, preferred majority rather than minority members, whereas infants ( N = 180) chose randomly between the two. Among adults ( N = 3,467), males also liked the majority more than females, and these coalitional preferences correlated robustly with political ideology. These results indicate that gendered motives for intergroup formidability are rooted in earliest childhood once children begin navigating peer relationships independently.

title: Algorithm-assisted personalized risk communication to encourage flu vaccination in the USA: three randomized field trials
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in healthcare to identify high-risk patients. Laboratory studies are mixed regarding patient attitudes towards AI use. Here we field-tested whether informing patients of their risk for influenza and its complications can serve as an effective behaviour-change intervention to increase vaccination, and whether disclosing AI use in the risk determination or providing personalized reasons for the algorithm’s prediction (a form of explainable AI) influence message effectiveness. We ran three preregistered randomized controlled trials with over 90,000 unique healthcare system patients in the USA (ClinicalTrials.gov identifiers: NCT04323137 , NCT05009251 and NCT05509283 ). Patients identified by a previously validated machine learning algorithm as being at high risk for influenza and related complications were randomized to be sent no message or one of several different messages encouraging influenza vaccination (the primary outcome). High-risk nudges increased vaccination: among patients informed of their high risk, vaccination was 1.1–1.4 percentage points (3.3–5.4%) higher than those simply reminded to get a vaccine, and 1.7–3.5 percentage points (3.3–14.7%) higher than non-messaged patients. Vaccination was similar across message arms that did versus did not disclose ‘algorithm’ involvement or its risk explanations, indicating that patients are neither averse to nor appreciative of algorithm use or explainability in this realistic health application. This work was partially funded by the National Institute on Aging of the National Institutes of Health under award number P30AG034532.

title: Contract incentives and behaviours of medical consultants in Ireland
abstract: In publicly funded healthcare systems that also allow private hospital treatment, there is often a concern that consultants might prioritize private patients. Here we examine how a 2014 reform in Ireland, which allowed public hospitals to accommodate private patients in public wards, affected consultant behaviours and patient outcomes. Using nationwide inpatient discharge data from 2009 to 2015 (2.3 million observations) and applying Little’s Law with a difference-in-differences method, we find no evidence that the share of private patients increased. We attribute this pattern to contracts requiring consultants to treat an additional three or four public patients for each treated private patient. The reform incentivized consultants to treat more public patients by shortening the lengths of stay for both public and private patients. However, such efficiency gains may come at the expense of care quality for public patients.

title: Recreational screen use and internalizing problems from preadolescence to young adulthood in a longitudinal twin cohort with co-twin comparison
abstract: The mental health impact of increasing recreational screen use among youth has raised substantial concerns, yet questions about causality remain unresolved. Here, leveraging a co-twin control design, we examined associations between screen use and internalizing problems from childhood to early adulthood among 21,797 Swedish twins, accounting for shared familial factors. Recreational screen use was associated with increased internalizing symptoms and clinical diagnosed depression and anxiety. However, these associations were substantially attenuated within discordant twin pairs and did not remain statistically significant after correction for multiple testing. These findings suggest that shared genetic and environmental factors partly explain the association between youth screen use and mental health. Although co-twin estimates provided limited evidence for clear causal effects, the association between heavy interactive screen use and clinical risk highlights the need to understand potential mechanisms linking digital behaviours and youth mental health.

title: Microdelays disrupt online learning
abstract: An ever-growing share of education happens on screens. We examine an overlooked feature of modern education: ‘microdelays’—brief loading lags that could hinder learners with slower internet connections. In two longitudinal quasi-experimental field studies, microdelays as short as 1–2 s predicted impaired learner engagement and achievement. When faced with microdelays, US primary and secondary school students ( N = 26,707) completed fewer online math assignments, took longer to complete assignments, were more likely to get distracted mid-task and earned lower scores. Likewise, when aspiring coders, primarily in Latin America ( N = 55,184), experienced microdelays, they spent less time actively engaged, multitasked more often, completed fewer lessons and were less likely to attain a key course milestone. Our results held across a range of model specifications, and leverage within-person variation in load times to support a causal interpretation. These findings identify microdelays as a hitherto-overlooked barrier in online learning.

title: Simulated responses from large language models are weak proxies for human economic preferences across 74 countries
abstract: Large-scale surveys are central to investigating economic preferences but are costly and slow. Can large language model (LLM)-simulated responses substitute for human survey data? We conducted a virtual Global Preference Survey, simulating six experimentally validated economic preferences for 67,201 matched human respondents across 74 countries. Across 20 LLM configurations with diverse prompts and robustness checks, we found systematic but modest individual-level alignment (87.5% of Spearman correlations have 95% confidence intervals (CIs) above zero), with LLMs recovering the direction of associations in 77.8% (95% CI, (71.6%, 83.1%); CI-based consistency ratio) of gender, age and cognitive-ability dimensions, but only 48.1% (95% CI, (45.1%, 51.2%)) of cultural dimensions. Ablation and error decompositions suggest weaker alignment when removing demographic information than when removing country labels, and in many models alignment is weaker in economically undeveloped and less digitally connected countries. LLM-simulated responses may recover some individual- and group-level patterns but are not yet reliable proxies for cross-national representative surveys in macro-level inference or policy evaluation.

title: Both selfish and prosocial actors distort their impact on others, but selfish-serving spin seems to spread
abstract: From consumers buying fair-trade products to policy makers funding science, people often do not know exactly how their actions will affect others. We show that selfish and prosocial actors alike may distort their impact in self-serving ways, but selfish-serving distortions catch on more readily than prosocial-serving distortions and increase followers’ selfishness.

title: Responsibilism and culture
abstract: Previous research has widely associated East Asian cultures with higher levels of collectivism, which is often measured through self-report scales that emphasize warmth and prosociality towards all people. Talhelm et al. developed a responsibilism scale that captures duties and responsibilities in close relationships.

title: Recognizing Indigenous peoples
abstract: Settler states increasingly offer Indigenous peoples symbolic recognition, such as land acknowledgements, instead of political power or resources, yet the effects of these gestures are untested. Peyton and McNamee’s experiments in the USA and Australia find that land acknowledgements raise awareness of Indigenous peoples but reduce interest in learning more.

title: Petition style changes with AI writing support but outcomes do not improve
abstract: In 2023, Change.org introduced an artificial intelligence (AI)-supported petition-drafting tool to their platform. With access to this tool, users’ petitions changed substantially, and their texts became more similar to one another. At the same time, overall petition outcomes did not improve, which shows the limits of AI integration into online advocacy communities.

title: The case for AI degrowth
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), as it currently unfolds, is incompatible with a sustainable transformation of the economy, which arguably requires degrowth. AI is the growth paradigm reborn — built on enclosed commons, powered by fossil energy, and driven by a competitive logic that makes precaution structurally impossible. Limits to AI growth are not technophobia; they are our best chance for a liveable future for all.

title: Use AI to heterogenize science
Trait judgements of faces using a task without word labels
abstract: People attribute psychological traits to faces. Previous research has typically elicited these judgements using specific words provided in advance by the experimenter (for example, ratings on competence or trustworthiness), raising questions about completeness (these tasks use a limited set of words) and generalizability (for example, across languages). Here we asked over 3,000 participants to spatially arrange unfamiliar faces based on perceived trait similarity, without providing any word labels. Using predominantly White faces, experiment 1 yielded five dimensions that we interpreted as approachability, gender-specific warmth, competence, morality and youthfulness. Using White, Black and Asian faces, experiment 2 also produced five dimensions, which showed prominent effects of stereotypes associated with race. Comparisons with four other studies that used word labels argue that approachability or warmth emerges as a universal evaluative factor that integrates multiple trait facets (such as trustworthiness, warmth and competence) into a single holistic dimension and that race and gender stereotypes emerge depending on the set of face stimuli used.

title: Motor abstraction training generalizes to the refinement of specific movement patterns
abstract: The ability to abstract the invariant structure of an experience while discarding incidental details underlies generalization across virtually every domain of human cognition, from vision and language to concept learning. Yet whether the motor system generates such abstractions and whether they causally contribute to skilled performance remain open questions. Here we introduce a paradigm in which human participants learned novel movement patterns by precisely copying unfamiliar handwritten characters. To examine the role of motor abstractions in this form of learning, participants were trained on markedly rotated versions of the characters, which recruited substantially different lower-level movements while still maintaining the relevant abstract movement trajectory. Across 11 experiments, abstraction training drove robust performance improvements that were comparable to having repetitive practice on the canonical form of each character. Moreover, this effect was largely motoric in nature: it did not require a visual template, sustained trajectory feedback or mental imagery, and was sensitive to the sequential structure of the movement trajectory. These findings establish a causal role for abstractions in motor learning, revealing that the motor system probably deploys abstractions in the earliest stages of skill acquisition.

title: Refining a new movement by practicing it upside down
abstract: In this study, participants improved at copying an unfamiliar alphabet character even though they only practiced writing rotated versions of it. The experiments reveal that the motor system can refine movements by creating an abstraction of their structure, and not only by repeating the same mechanical muscle commands.

title: Privileged representational axes in biological and artificial neural networks
abstract: How do neurons code information? Recent work emphasizes the geometry and information content of population codes, using measures that are blind to the native tunings (or ‘axes’) of neural responses. But might these representational axes matter, with some privileged systematically over others? We developed methods to test for alignment of neural tuning across brains and deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs). Across both vision and audition, both brains and DCNNs consistently favoured certain axes for representing the natural world. Moreover, the representational axes of DCNNs trained on natural inputs were aligned to those in perceptual cortices, such that axis-sensitive model–brain similarity metrics better differentiated competing models of biological sensory systems. We further show that coding schemes that privilege certain axes can facilitate task performance, reduce downstream wiring costs and improve generalization. These results motivate a new framework for understanding neural tuning in biological and artificial networks and its computational benefits.

title: Large language models for computational social science
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are transforming computational social science. This Review examines how LLMs now serve four distinct research roles: subjects that simulate human behaviour, assistants that automate analysis, collaborators that generate hypotheses and evaluators that audit and improve research quality. We analyse recent advances across sociology, political science, psychology, anthropology, economics and related fields, revealing how LLMs accelerate discovery while creating new methodological paradigms. This transformation arrives as society itself becomes saturated with artificial intelligence agents—making LLMs both our research tools and authentic research subjects. Yet fundamental challenges persist. LLMs struggle with causal inference and raise urgent ethical concerns about privacy and misinformation, and their ability to reproduce social complexity remains uneven and unproven. We identify critical research directions for harnessing LLMs’ potential while addressing their limitations. As artificial intelligence reshapes human society, understanding this transformation requires the very tools driving it—a recursive challenge that will define the future of social science.

title: Generative AI and the temporary upskilling of knowledge workers
abstract: Upskilling often refers to the process by which workers acquire and expand their skills, enabling them to perform different types of work as market demands change. Here we demonstrate that generative artificial intelligence can act as an ‘exoskeleton’, enhancing workers’ capabilities when attempting new skills, but these gains depend on continued technology use. We run a randomized controlled trial on upskilling by providing management consultants ( N = 487) access and training in using ChatGPT to solve data science tasks outside their skill sets, which cannot be independently solved by ChatGPT. The treated workers scored higher than the control group on three tasks, although we can reject the hypothesis that they performed as well as expert data scientists. We find no evidence that treated workers are better at answering technical questions without ChatGPT post-experiment, suggesting that their demonstrated technical capabilities do not imply knowledge acquisition.

title: Turing-like tests for language and vision demonstrate a narrowing gap between humans and AI
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in daily life, ascertaining whether an agent is human is critical. Here we systematically benchmark AI’s ability to imitate humans in three language tasks (image captioning, word association and conversation) and three vision tasks (colour estimation, object detection and attention prediction), collecting data from n = 636 humans and 37 AI agents. We also conducted 72,191 Turing-like tests with 1,916 human judges and 10 AI judges. Current AIs are approaching the ability to convincingly impersonate humans and deceive human judges in both language and vision. Even simple AI judges outperformed humans in distinguishing AI from human responses. Imitation ability showed minimal correlation with conventional AI performance metrics, suggesting that passing as human is an important independent evaluation criterion. The large-scale Turing-like datasets and metrics introduced here offer valuable benchmarks for assessing human-likeness in AI and highlight the importance of rigorous, quantitative imitation tests for AI development.

title: Within-family heritability estimates for behavioural and disease phenotypes from 500,000 sibling pairs of diverse ancestries
abstract: Quantification of the direct effect of genetic variation on human behavioural traits is important for understanding between-individual variation in socioeconomic and health outcomes but estimates of their heritability can be biased by between-family indirect genetic effects. By contrast, using within-family variation in DNA sharing is robust to most confounding factors including shared environmental effects and population stratification. Yet, accurate estimates for most traits are not available using this design, and none for non-European ancestry populations. Here we analyse approximately 500,000 sibling pairs with diverse genetic ancestries and obtain within-family heritability estimates for 14 phenotypes, including two well-studied model traits: height (0.70 ± 0.03) and BMI (0.49 ± 0.03). For behaviour, we find significant within-family heritability for smoking initiation (0.34 ± 0.05), alcohol consumption (0.18 ± 0.04), number of children (0.27 ± 0.11) and personality (‘talk versus listen’, 0.48 ± 0.13). In addition, we estimated large heritability for type 2 diabetes (0.43 ± 0.06) and asthma (0.34 ± 0.06), whose risk factors include behavioural traits. Overall, we show concordant estimates across ancestry groups and highlight a significant contribution of shared environmental effects for behaviour and type 2 diabetes risk, which may have inflated between-family estimates. Altogether, our results provide within-family evidence that genetic variation is associated with variation in complex traits, common disease and exposures. Our heritability estimates are concordant across genetic ancestries, lower than those from twin-based studies, yet larger than has been accounted for by genome-wide association studies so far.

title: AI governance needs to consider users’ emotional responses
abstract: People will often trust or distrust an artificial intelligence (AI) output because of how it makes them feel, rather than how reliable it is. AI governance frameworks should require that platforms disclose design choices that target user emotions, allow users control over these, and include features aimed to calibrate trust.

title: Decredentialed jobs and upward mobility among non-college workers in the USA
abstract: Prominent employers are increasingly dropping college degree requirements when hiring. Does this provide upward mobility for non-college workers? Matching job postings to 446,500 job starts in US administrative data from 2011 to 2021, we show that employers reduced the share of postings requiring a degree by more than 10%. Non-college workers who move to decredentialed jobs earn 12 log points more than matched workers moving to never-credentialed jobs ( β = 0.124; 95% confidence interval, (0.042, 0.206)), around US$4,600 per year—a premium that endures for at least five years. These hires are more likely to be Black, Hispanic and female than the workers they replace. Employers also benefit, as removing degree requirements reduces labour costs. Yet most employers that drop requirements do not hire non-college workers (non-college hiring rises 1.2 percentage points; 95% confidence interval, (0.5, 2.0)). Decredentialing is a promising tool for social mobility, but only when employers follow through.

title: Preprimary education laws and women’s empowerment later in life
abstract: Across nearly 6.7 million women in 117 low- and middle-income countries, eligibility under national preprimary education laws was associated with higher educational enrolment and completion, more gender-egalitarian attitudes, more favourable empowerment-related behaviours and greater reproductive autonomy.

title: Preprimary education laws and women’s gender attitudes, empowerment and reproductive autonomy in 117 low- and middle-income countries
abstract: Preprimary education is central to the global education agenda, including Sustainable Development Goal 4.2. Despite global momentum in low- and middle-income countries, cross-national evidence on long-term outcomes associated with preprimary education legislation remains limited. Here we applied a matrix-completion approach with subgroup and sensitivity analyses using 495 nationally representative surveys from 1990 to 2024, covering nearly 6.7 million women across 117 countries. Eligibility under the legislation was associated with higher educational enrolment and completion, and with more gender-egalitarian attitudes, more favourable empowerment-related behaviours and greater reproductive autonomy. For example, eligibility was associated with higher female primary-school enrolment (1.21 percentage points (pp); 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.52 to 1.91; P < 0.001) and completion (0.75 pp; 95% CI 0.24 to 1.25; P = 0.004), greater disapproval of wife-beating (1.04 pp; 95% CI 0.53 to 1.56; P < 0.001), greater participation in decisions about husbands’ earnings (3.25 pp; 95% CI 2.50 to 4.00; P < 0.001) and greater ever use of contraception (2.96 pp; 95% CI 2.33 to 3.59; P < 0.001). Eligibility under the legislation was also associated with lower rates of adolescent childbearing (−2.41 pp; 95% CI −2.67 to −2.14; P < 0.001) and child marriage (−0.43 pp; 95% CI −0.71 to −0.15; P = 0.003). These findings provide cross-national evidence directly relevant to ongoing policy discussions surrounding Sustainable Development Goal 4.2 and broader global development agendas, while emphasizing the importance of implementation capacity and equitable system expansion.
